text: Does a high IQ grant someone special insight into the Bible and Christianity?
Hey everybody, I'm Dan Mlullen. I'm a scholar of the Bible and religion. And recently, a man named Yong Hun Kim has been getting a lot of attention for
leveraging what he claims to be the highest IQ ever, 276, to endorse and validate Christian faith claims. So,
here are a few recent examples.
Yesterday he tweeted, "As the world's highest IQ record holder, I trust that Christianity offers the clearest way to
understand and experience God. Through the teachings of Jesus, we can find the most complete and true knowledge of God,
who is love and salvation." The day before that, he tweeted, "As the world's highest IQ holder, I believe the Bible is the perfect, eternal, and final word
of God. Therefore, the Bible doesn't need to be updated. The world needs to catch up." And then two days before
that, he tweeted, "As the world's highest IQ record holder, I believe that Jesus Christ is God, the way and the truth, and the life." Now, I have a few
concerns here. Chief among them is the fact that not only are most of these claims not actually in the Bible,
they're Christian dogmas, but they're all dogmas. These are not conclusions anyone arrives at after a careful,
critical, and informed interrogation of the data. These are dogmas precisely because they're not really supported by
the data. They're things that one is either conditioned from childhood to accept as true or things that they have
decided to accept as true. They are credences onto which one signs in order to gain access to the power and
resources made available by membership in the groups that identify these things as their identity markers. There's
nothing about a high IQ that grants anyone special insight into the Bible or into Christian theology. And this individual has certainly given no
indication that they have any advanced training or expertise in anything related to the Bible or theology. the
fact that they continue to leverage their claim of having the highest IQ ever as the authorizer validator of
these claims makes it clear this is a pretty transparent appeal to an irrelevant authority which raises the question of why someone would be doing
this. And one interpretation is that this is part of an attempt to curry favor with Christian nationalists either
for personal or broader entrepreneurial uh or other kinds of goals. So this individual is retweeting an awful lot of
large right-wing authoritarian and Christian nationalist accounts like Charlie Kirk, like MAGA Voice, and like many, many others. So, this could be
part of the kind of attempt that folks like Joe Rogan and Jordan Peterson and Russell Brand have made to leverage
their celebrity by endorsing Christian nationalist identity markers so that they can gain greater access to power
and resources. It could be more personal because this is an individual with a more global audience who is not so
focused entirely on Christian nationalism itself. I don't know what's going on in Kim's mind, but there are no
data that support these Christian identity markers. This is an attempt to leverage one's IQ to try to authorize
and validate those Christian identity markers, those dogmas in the absence of
any actual data. And that to me is rather problematic. But whatever Yung Hun Kim is trying to do here, what
they're not doing is providing any kind of argument or saying anything particularly insightful. And the fit for this video has been The Man Without Fear.
